concept.name: CAP Theorem & PACELC Consistency Models

reviewRecord.reviewNotes: Seeded for SPEC-062 pillar coverage matrix.

concept.tagline: Navigating the Partition (C vs. A) and Else-Normal (Latency vs. Consistency) trade-offs across distributed data stores.
concept.purpose: Build a progressive mental model of CAP and PACELC—from linearizability vs. eventual consistency to quorum math and hybrid multi-store architectures.

spark.summary: CAP proves a distributed data store cannot simultaneously guarantee linearizability (C) and 100% availability (A) during a network partition (P); PACELC extends this to normal operation, forcing a choice between latency (L) and consistency (C) even when no partition exists.
spark.keyTakeaway: Because network partitions are inevitable, the real-world design choice is not 'CP vs AP'—it is which data requires linearizable PC/EC quorums and which can tolerate PA/EL eventual or causal consistency.
spark.byteSummary:
**Core Mechanics:** Eric Brewer's **CAP Theorem** (Gilbert & Lynch, 2002) proves that when a network partition (**P**) splits a distributed store, it must choose between: **Consistency (C — Linearizability)**: Every read returns the most recent.

**Visual & Structural Flow:** Depicts 3-Region Cluster Under Network Partition (N1/N2 vs. Isolated N3) (N1 Leader (US-East) -> N2 (US-Central) -> N3 (US-West, Isolated)); Stale Read Risk on Async Replica vs. Linearizable Quorum Read (Writer -> Primary / Leader -> Async Replica -> Reader); Edge Gateway -> PA/EL Carts & Catalog vs. PC/EC Payments & Inventory (Global Edge GW -> PA/EL Store (Carts) -> PC/EC Store (Ledger) -> CDC Event Bus).

**Trade-Offs & Production:** Compare replication protocols, write latency, and partition behavior across major engines. A global e-commerce platform keeps **inventory, payments, and auth** on a PC/EC store (**Spanner / CockroachDB**) while serving **product catalog, session carts (CRDTs), and user.

**Failure Modes & Application:** Explore CAP/PACELC trade-offs, quorum tuning, read-your-own-writes, and CRDT conflict resolution.

learningJourney.title: What are CAP and PACELC
learningJourney.explanation:
Eric Brewer's **CAP Theorem** (Gilbert & Lynch, 2002) proves that when a network partition (**P**) splits a distributed store, it must choose between:
- **Consistency (C — Linearizability)**: Every read returns the most recent completed write in real-time order (or an error).
- **Availability (A)**: Every non-failing node returns a non-error response, even if stale.

**PACELC** (Daniel Abadi, 2012) adds the missing half: **if P** (partition), choose **A or C**; **else (E)** (normal operation), choose **L (latency) or C (consistency)**.

sectionDiagram.title: 3-Region Cluster Under Network Partition (N1/N2 vs. Isolated N3)

cards.label: PC/EC (etcd, Spanner)
cards.detail: Majority (N1+N2) commits $80; isolated N3 rejects writes/reads to preserve linearizability.

cards.label: PA/EL (Dynamo, Cassandra)
cards.detail: Isolated N3 still accepts writes locally, risking divergent values reconciled later via CRDTs/LWW.

cards.label: Normal-Op Latency Tax
cards.detail: Even without a partition, PC/EC pays cross-node RTT on writes while PA/EL responds locally.

sectionDiagram.summary: During a partition, PC/EC fences the minority side while PA/EL stays available on both sides and reconciles later.

learningJourney.title: Why we need Consistency Models (and how naive assumptions fail)
learningJourney.explanation:
Treating 'CP vs AP' as a binary switch leads to three expensive production failures:

1. **Quorum Without Linearizability**: Setting $W + R > N$ (e.g., $N=3, W=2, R=2$) ensures overlap in Dynamo-style stores, *but* without leader/read-repair coordination, concurrent writes + partial propagation can still violate linearizability.
2. **Clock-Skew LWW Overwrites**: Using Last-Write-Wins (LWW) with wall clocks when NTP drifts 150 ms lets older writes silently overwrite newer writes.
3. **Asymmetric / Gray Partitions**: N1 can reach N2, N2 can reach N3, but N1 cannot reach N3—breaking naive health checks.

sectionDiagram.title: Stale Read Risk on Async Replica vs. Linearizable Quorum Read
sectionDiagram.summary: Reading from async replicas violates read-your-own-writes; linearizable reads require quorum ReadIndex or valid leader leases.

ideas.title: Consistency Hierarchy
ideas.description: Linearizability (strongest, real-time) > Sequential > Causal (preserves happens-before) > Eventual (converges if writes stop).

ideas.title: TrueTime & HLC
ideas.description: Google Spanner uses GPS/atomic TrueTime [-7ms, +7ms] for external consistency; CockroachDB uses Hybrid Logical Clocks (HLC).

learningJourney.title: Where Different PACELC Classes belong in one system
learningJourney.explanation: Production architectures rarely pick one PACELC class globally—they place each domain on the store whose guarantees match its invariants.

benefits: Linearizable/serializable guarantees for billing, inventory, identity, and leader election.
costs: 10-85 ms write RTT across zones/regions; minority partition rejects writes.

benefits: Sub-5 ms local writes and high availability for carts, sessions, feeds, and telemetry.
costs: Eventual consistency requires CRDTs, idempotency, or read-repair to resolve conflicts.

benefits: Fast local reads when healthy (EL), strict quorum/majority writes when configured.
costs: Default eventual reads can return stale values right after a write unless ConsistentRead=true.

learningJourney.purpose: Scope boundary: identify where this pattern fits best and where simpler or async alternatives win.

learningJourney.title: How Quorums, Session Consistency, and Conflict Resolution are managed
learningJourney.explanation:
Bridge consistency and latency in application code:

1. **Read-Your-Own-Writes**: Pin a user's reads to the primary (or pass a monotonic LSN/commit token) for a few seconds after their write.
2. **Never Use Wall-Clock LWW for Critical State**: Use CRDTs (OR-Set, PN-Counter) or HLC/version vectors instead of raw timestamps.
3. **Leader Leases / ReadIndex**: In Raft stores, serve linearizable reads via `ReadIndex` without writing a log entry.

learningJourney.title: Alternatives: PACELC Matrix Across Real Databases
learningJourney.explanation: Compare replication protocols, write latency, and partition behavior across major engines.

benefits: 2-10 ms intra-region linearizable writes; fencing via monotonic revision/zxid.
costs: Small metadata scale only; minority partition refuses all writes.

benefits: Horizontally sharded distributed ACID SQL with HLC / TrueTime.
costs: 20-85 ms cross-region write RTT; sensitive to clock-skew bounds.

benefits: Multi-master availability even during cross-region splits; low local latency.
costs: Conflicts under concurrent writes require LWW, CRDTs, or conditional writes (LWT).

learningJourney.title: Production example: Hybrid PC/EC Core + PA/EL Edge Store
learningJourney.explanation: A global e-commerce platform keeps **inventory, payments, and auth** on a PC/EC store (**Spanner / CockroachDB**) while serving **product catalog, session carts (CRDTs), and user feeds** from a PA/EL store (**DynamoDB Global Tables / Redis**).

sectionDiagram.title: Edge Gateway -> PA/EL Carts & Catalog vs. PC/EC Payments & Inventory

cards.label: Zero Over-Selling
cards.detail: Inventory decrement and payment capture execute in PC/EC ACID transactions.

cards.label: Always-On Carts
cards.detail: Shopping carts use PA/EL add-wins CRDT sets so users can add items even during a region split.

cards.label: Causal Session Tokens
cards.detail: Write responses return an LSN/token so immediate follow-up reads see own writes.

sectionDiagram.summary: Splitting PC/EC correctness from PA/EL availability gives both zero double-spends and 99.999% shopping uptime.

_recommendedProblem.title: Active-Active Multi-Master Split-Brain Recovery
_recommendedProblem.prompt: Redesign an active-active multi-master relational replication pipeline between us-east-1 and eu-west-1 (6,000 writes/sec, 85 ms WAN RTT, < 15 ms p99 local commit) so a 9-minute transatlantic partition and 180-250 ms NTP clock skew never cause silent Last-Write-Wins (LWW) overwrites.
